headline: Burnham pledges to scrap pension triple lock to fund National Care Service

terms.meaning: A promise that the state pension rises each year by the highest of inflation, average earnings growth or 2.5 per cent.
A proposed service giving free personal care to older people, run on NHS-style principles.
Changing the way votes are turned into seats in Parliament.

levels.headline: Burnham pledges to scrap pension triple lock to fund National Care Service
levels.body:
Andy Burnham told Labour's conference that the party will drop the state pension triple lock in its next manifesto, using the savings to pay for a new National Care Service.
Under the plan, from 2030 the state pension would rise in line with inflation or 2.5 per cent, ending the automatic link with average earnings that the triple lock provides. Party analysis suggests the change would save the government £15bn a year from 2040.
The National Care Service would be set up in the next parliament and would provide free personal care for older people. It would be founded on the same principles as the NHS, where everyone contributes and everyone is covered.
Mr Burnham also announced a National Commission on Electoral Reform, so that the voting system better gives power to people in every postcode. All parties would be invited to take part, along with community groups, trade unions, businesses, faith groups and voters, and it would report before the next general election.
The triple lock, introduced in 2010, has become one of the most expensive and politically sensitive features of the pensions system.
levels.why: Pensions and social care affect millions of families, and the triple lock has long been politically hard to change.

levels.headline: Burnham to drop triple lock and create National Care Service
levels.body:
Andy Burnham used Labour's conference to announce that the party will drop the state pension triple lock in its next manifesto and use the money to create a National Care Service.
From 2030, the state pension would rise in line with inflation or 2.5 per cent, rather than also being tied to average earnings. Party analysis says this would save the government £15bn a year from 2040.
The new service would be created in the next parliament. It would offer free personal care for older people and be built on the NHS principle that everyone contributes and everyone is covered.
Mr Burnham also said Labour would launch a National Commission on Electoral Reform, inviting all parties, unions, businesses, faith groups, community groups and voters to help look at the voting system. It would report before the next general election.
The triple lock has been popular with pensioners but costly for the Treasury, so any move to end it is likely to be closely scrutinised.
levels.why: Any change to pensions is politically sensitive, and the care plan would be one of the biggest public spending commitments in years.

levels.headline: Burnham pledges to end triple lock and fund free personal care
levels.body:
Andy Burnham has announced that Labour would drop the state pension triple lock in its next manifesto to pay for a new National Care Service.
The triple lock is the promise that the state pension rises each year by the highest of inflation, average earnings or 2.5 per cent. Under Mr Burnham's plan, from 2030 it would instead rise in line with inflation or 2.5 per cent. Party analysis suggests this would save £15bn a year by 2040.
The National Care Service would give older people free personal care, such as help with washing, dressing and eating. It would work like the NHS, with everyone paying in and everyone covered. It would start in the next parliament.
He also announced a National Commission on Electoral Reform, which would look at how votes are turned into seats. Every party would be invited to join, and it would report before the next general election.
Critics and supporters are likely to argue over whether pensioners would lose out.
levels.why: Many families struggle with the cost of care, and pensions are a major part of government spending.

levels.headline: Labour plans to scrap pension triple lock and create free care service
levels.body:
Andy Burnham has said Labour will drop the state pension triple lock in its next manifesto so that it can pay for a National Care Service.
The triple lock guarantees that pensions go up by whichever is highest out of inflation, wages or 2.5 per cent. From 2030, Mr Burnham says, pensions would rise in line with inflation or 2.5 per cent. Labour's own analysis says that would save £15bn a year from 2040.
The care service would provide free personal care for older people and would be based on the NHS idea that everyone pays in and everyone is covered. It would be set up in the next parliament.
Mr Burnham also announced a National Commission on Electoral Reform. All parties would be asked to take part, along with unions, businesses, faith groups, community groups and voters. It would report before the next general election.
The announcements were made at Labour's party conference.
levels.why: The plan shows how Labour might pay for care, but it means changing a pension promise many older people rely on.

levels.headline: Burnham wants to change pensions to pay for care
levels.body:
Andy Burnham has announced a big plan at Labour's conference. He says Labour would end the triple lock on state pensions and use the money to build a National Care Service.
The triple lock is a rule that makes the state pension go up each year by the biggest of three things: prices rising, wages rising, or 2.5 per cent. Under Mr Burnham's plan, from 2030 it would go up with prices or by 2.5 per cent. That would stop wages from being part of the rule. Labour says it would save £15bn a year by 2040.
The care service would give older people free personal care. It would work like the NHS, where everyone pays in and everyone is looked after. It would begin in the next parliament.
Mr Burnham also wants a National Commission on Electoral Reform to look at how we vote. It would report before the next general election.
levels.why: Care costs worry many families, and this plan changes how pensions are set to help pay for it.

levels.headline: Labour plan: end the pension triple lock, create a free care service
levels.body:
Andy Burnham has said what Labour would do if it wins the next election. It would stop using the triple lock for the state pension and start a National Care Service.
The state pension is money the government pays older people. The triple lock means it goes up each year by the biggest of prices, wages or 2.5 per cent. Mr Burnham says from 2030 it would go up with prices or by 2.5 per cent. Labour says this would save £15bn a year by 2040.
The money would help pay for free personal care for older people. This means help with things like washing and getting dressed. Everyone would pay in, and everyone would be covered, like the NHS.
Mr Burnham also plans a National Commission on Electoral Reform. It would look at how votes become seats in Parliament. All parties would be asked to join.
levels.why: Free care could help many families, but the pension change might mean smaller rises for pensioners.

levels.headline: Labour says it would change pensions to pay for care
levels.body:
A man called Andy Burnham has told his party, Labour, about a plan. If Labour wins the next election, it wants to change how the state pension goes up and to start a care service.
The state pension is money the government gives to older people. At the moment a rule called the triple lock says it must rise each year by prices, wages or 2.5 per cent, whichever is biggest. Labour wants it to rise with prices or by 2.5 per cent from 2030. Labour says this would save £15bn a year by 2040.
The care service would give older people free help with things like washing and getting dressed. Everyone would pay taxes to support it, like the NHS.
The plan also includes a group to look at how we vote. All parties would be asked to join it.
levels.why: It matters because it affects how much older people get and how care for them is paid for.

levels.headline: A plan to pay for care for older people
levels.body:
Andy Burnham is a politician in the Labour Party. He has a new plan to help older people who need care.
Some older people need help with washing, dressing or eating. A National Care Service would give them this help for free. Everyone would pay into it through taxes. It would work like the NHS.
To pay for it, Mr Burnham wants to change how the state pension grows. The state pension is money the government gives older people each month. Now there is a rule called the triple lock. It makes the pension go up each year by prices, wages or 2.5 per cent, whichever is biggest. Mr Burnham wants it to go up by prices or 2.5 per cent instead, from 2030.
He also wants a group to think about how we vote. Every party would be asked to join.
levels.why: It matters because it is about how we look after older people and how we pay for it.

levels.headline: A new plan to help older people
levels.body:
A politician called Andy Burnham has a plan. It is for older people who need help at home.
Some older people cannot wash or dress by themselves. Someone has to help them. That is called care. Today many families have to pay for it. Mr Burnham wants care to be free. He calls the plan the National Care Service. It would work like the NHS. Everyone gives a little money, and everyone gets help when they need it.
To pay for it, he wants to change a rule about pensions. A pension is money the government gives to older people. The rule is called the triple lock. It makes pensions go up every year. Mr Burnham wants pensions to go up a little more slowly. Then there would be money left for care.
He also wants people to talk about how we vote.
levels.why: It matters because families need help caring for older people, and money has to come from somewhere.

levels.headline: Helping grandparents when they need care
levels.body:
Imagine your grandparents get older and need some help. Maybe they need help getting dressed or making lunch. That is called care.
A grown-up called Andy Burnham has a plan. He says that help should be free for everyone who needs it. It would be like how doctors and hospitals in the NHS are there for everybody.
But free help costs money. Think of a class party where everyone puts in a little pocket money to buy snacks. Mr Burnham says some of the money could come from changing how pensions go up. A pension is money older people get every month. Right now it goes up by a set rule each year. He wants the rule to be a bit different.
Some people will like the plan and some will not. That is how grown-ups decide things.
levels.why: It matters because looking after older people kindly is important, and grown-ups must decide how to pay for it.

headline: Iran says Hormuz stays closed until US meets conditions as war talks stall

terms.meaning: A narrow waterway between Iran and Oman through which a large share of the world's oil is shipped.
Processing uranium to make it more powerful, either for power stations or, at high levels, for weapons.
The main international benchmark price for oil.

levels.headline: Iran says Hormuz stays closed until US meets conditions as war talks stall
levels.body:
Iran says the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until the United States meets seven conditions based on a June memorandum of understanding, as talks to end the seven-month war remain deadlocked.
Iran's Parliament Speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, set out the position. Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman said reopening the strait is the main focus of its negotiations, and that the latest US proposal was almost identical to earlier ones, with Washington still concentrating on the nuclear issue.
US Vice President JD Vance said Iran must meaningfully reduce its uranium enrichment capacity, asking why Iran needs 60% enriched fuel if it does not want a nuclear weapon. President Trump said a decision on Iran is imminent, either the easy way or the hard way, while Iran's foreign minister said Tehran is more prepared than before.
Brent crude was trading near $102.60.
levels.why: The closure of the strait and the stalled talks keep oil prices high, which feeds into energy bills and inflation worldwide.

levels.headline: Iran-US talks deadlocked over Hormuz and enrichment
levels.body:
Iran has said the Strait of Hormuz will stay closed until the United States meets seven conditions drawn from a June memorandum of understanding. The two sides are trying to end a war that is now seven months old.
Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf made the announcement. Iran's Foreign Ministry says Hormuz is its main focus and describes the latest US proposal as nearly the same as earlier ones, because Washington keeps focusing on Iran's nuclear programme.
Vice President JD Vance said Iran needs to cut its uranium enrichment capacity in a meaningful way, and questioned the need for 60% enriched fuel. President Trump said a decision was imminent, either the easy way or the hard way. Iran's foreign minister said Tehran is more prepared than before.
Brent crude traded near $102.60.
levels.why: With the strait closed, a key route for global oil is disrupted, so the dispute affects prices everywhere.

levels.headline: Iran says Strait of Hormuz will stay shut until US meets its conditions
levels.body:
Iran says the Strait of Hormuz will stay closed until the United States meets seven conditions. These are based on an agreement signed in June. The war between Iran and the United States has now lasted seven months.
Iran's Parliament Speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said this. Iran's Foreign Ministry said the strait is the main topic in talks. It also said the latest US offer was almost the same as earlier ones, because the US keeps focusing on nuclear issues.
US Vice President JD Vance said Iran must reduce how much uranium it can enrich. He asked why Iran needs fuel enriched to 60% if it does not want a nuclear weapon. President Trump said a decision is close. Iran's foreign minister said Iran is more prepared than before.
Oil was priced at about $102.60 a barrel.
levels.why: A large share of the world's oil usually passes through the strait, so what happens there affects fuel and energy costs.

levels.headline: Talks to end the Iran war are stuck over Hormuz and nuclear fuel
levels.body:
Iran says it will keep the Strait of Hormuz closed until the United States meets seven conditions. These come from an agreement made in June. The war between the two countries is now seven months old.
Iran's Parliament Speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said so. Iran's Foreign Ministry says reopening the strait is the main thing it wants to discuss. It says the latest US proposal is almost identical to earlier ones, because Washington keeps focusing on Iran's nuclear programme.
US Vice President JD Vance said Iran must meaningfully reduce its ability to enrich uranium. President Trump said a decision on Iran is coming soon and warned of an easy way or a hard way. Iran's foreign minister said Tehran is better prepared than before.
Oil was trading around $102.60.
levels.why: It matters because the war and the closed waterway keep oil prices high.

levels.headline: Iran and the US cannot agree, and a key sea route is still closed
levels.body:
Iran and the United States have been at war for seven months. They are now trying to agree how to stop it, but the talks are stuck.
Iran says a narrow stretch of sea, called the Strait of Hormuz, will stay closed until the US meets seven conditions. A lot of the world's oil normally travels through it. The conditions come from an agreement made in June. The US says Iran must cut how much uranium it can enrich. Uranium is the material used for nuclear power and, when it is enriched a lot, for bombs.
US Vice President JD Vance asked why Iran needs very strongly enriched fuel if it does not want a bomb. President Trump said a decision is close. Iran says it is more ready than before.
Oil costs about $102.60 a barrel.
levels.why: It matters because oil prices affect petrol, heating and the cost of many goods.

levels.headline: Why talks to end the Iran war are stuck
levels.body:
Iran and the United States have been at war for seven months. They are now talking about how to end it, but they cannot agree.
One problem is the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow stretch of sea that much of the world's oil normally travels through. Iran says it will keep it closed until the US meets seven conditions, which come from an agreement made in June. Iran says that reopening the strait is its main focus.
The US is more concerned with Iran's nuclear work. US Vice President JD Vance says Iran must cut how much uranium it can enrich, and asked why it needs fuel enriched to 60% if it does not want a nuclear weapon. President Trump said a decision is close, while Iran says it is more prepared than before.
Oil costs about $102.60 a barrel.
levels.why: It matters because oil prices affect petrol, heating and food costs around the world.

levels.headline: The Iran war talks are stuck
levels.body:
Iran and the United States are at war. It has lasted seven months. The two countries are talking about how to end it, but they cannot agree.
One problem is the Strait of Hormuz. This is a narrow piece of sea where lots of the world's oil ships pass. Iran says it will keep it closed until the US does seven things. The US wants something else. It wants Iran to make less enriched uranium. This is a material that can be used to make power or, if it is very strong, a weapon.
US Vice President JD Vance said Iran does not need very strong uranium if it does not want a weapon. President Trump said a decision is close. Iran says it is ready.
Oil costs about $102.60 a barrel.
levels.why: It matters because high oil prices make petrol and heating cost more.

levels.headline: Two countries disagree and a sea route stays closed
levels.body:
The United States and Iran have been fighting a war for seven months. Now they are talking about ending it, but they are stuck.
Iran controls one side of a narrow sea passage called the Strait of Hormuz. Many ships carrying oil to the rest of the world usually go through it. Iran says it will keep it closed until the US agrees to seven things. The US says it wants Iran to make less of a special material called enriched uranium. In strong forms, it can be used to make dangerous weapons.
The US Vice President, JD Vance, said Iran does not need the very strong kind if it does not want weapons. The US president said he would decide soon.
Oil is now costing about $102.60 a barrel.
levels.why: It matters because oil is used for petrol and heating, so its price touches everyone.

levels.headline: A big argument between two countries
levels.body:
Two countries, the United States and Iran, have been fighting for seven months. Now their leaders are talking about stopping. But they do not agree.
Iran says a narrow stretch of sea will stay closed. Lots of oil ships normally sail through it. Oil is used to make petrol for cars. Iran says the sea will stay closed until the US does seven things.
The US wants Iran to stop making a very strong material that could be used for dangerous weapons. A leader in the US asked why Iran needs it if it does not want weapons.
Because the sea is closed, oil is costing more, about $102.60 a barrel.
Nobody knows yet how it will end.
levels.why: It matters because when oil costs more, many things cost more.

levels.headline: Two children and one blocked path
levels.body:
Imagine two children are arguing in the playground. One of them is standing in a narrow doorway that everyone needs to use. The other child says, move out of the way. The first child says, only if you do what I ask first.
That is a bit like what is happening between Iran and the United States. They have been fighting for seven months. Iran is keeping a narrow sea path closed, called the Strait of Hormuz. Many ships carrying oil need it. Iran says it will open it when the US agrees to seven things.
The US wants Iran to make less of a special material that could be used for dangerous weapons.
Because the path is blocked, oil costs more, and that makes petrol more expensive.
levels.why: It matters because the blocked path makes oil cost more for everyone.

headline: Healey faces tight margins as Autumn Budget approaches on 28 October

terms.meaning: The gap between what the government plans to borrow and the limit set by its own rules.
The Chancellor's yearly statement on taxes and public spending.
Money the government raises because it spends more than it collects in tax.

levels.headline: Healey faces tight margins as Autumn Budget approaches on 28 October
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey will deliver the Autumn Budget on 28 October with very little room for manoeuvre, according to reports from September.
His fiscal headroom, the gap between his plans and the limits set by the government's own fiscal rules, has reportedly shrunk to as little as £5bn. Borrowing is running £8.1bn above forecast. This is Mr Healey's first Budget as Chancellor, after he replaced Rachel Reeves in July 2026, so he has inherited fiscal rules she introduced.
He has promised not to raise income tax, employee National Insurance or VAT. Those three taxes raise most of the government's revenue, so ruling out rises leaves fewer options for closing any gap.
The Budget is expected to cover tax, pensions, benefits and savings. Higher energy prices linked to the Middle East conflict have also made the economic backdrop harder.
levels.why: A thin margin means the Chancellor may have to choose between tax rises elsewhere, spending cuts or changing the rules.

levels.headline: Autumn Budget on 28 October: Healey has little room to manoeuvre
levels.body:
John Healey, the Chancellor, will present the Autumn Budget on 28 October, his first since replacing Rachel Reeves in July 2026.
Reports in September said his fiscal headroom has shrunk to as little as £5bn. That is the cushion between planned borrowing and the limits of the government's fiscal rules, which he inherited from Ms Reeves. Borrowing is also running £8.1bn above forecast.
Mr Healey has promised not to raise income tax, employee National Insurance or VAT. Because those are the biggest sources of tax revenue, the promise narrows his choices.
The Budget is expected to affect tax, pensions, benefits, savings and household budgets. The rise in energy costs linked to the conflict in the Middle East adds to the pressure.
levels.why: With so little room, almost any change to tax or spending could have a big effect on households.

levels.headline: Chancellor has little spare money ahead of the 28 October Budget
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey will give the Autumn Budget on 28 October. It will be his first, after he replaced Rachel Reeves in July 2026.
Reports in September suggest the government has very little spare room under its own borrowing rules. This room is called fiscal headroom, and it may be as small as £5bn. On top of that, the government is borrowing £8.1bn more than forecast.
Mr Healey has promised not to raise income tax, employees' National Insurance or VAT. These taxes bring in a huge share of government income, so leaving them alone makes it harder to find extra money.
The Budget is expected to cover taxes, pensions, benefits and savings. Higher energy prices because of the conflict in the Middle East are also making things harder.
levels.why: It shows how tight the government's finances are, which affects taxes and public services.

levels.headline: Healey's first Budget comes with very little spare cash
levels.body:
John Healey will give his first Budget as Chancellor on 28 October. He took over from Rachel Reeves in July 2026.
Reports from September say the government has just £5bn or even less of what is called fiscal headroom. That is the safety margin before it breaks its own borrowing rules. The government is also borrowing £8.1bn more than it forecast.
Mr Healey has said he will not raise income tax, employee National Insurance or VAT. Those are the biggest taxes, so promising to leave them alone reduces his options.
The Budget is expected to include changes to tax, pensions, benefits and savings. Energy bills have risen because of the war in the Middle East, which makes the task harder.
levels.why: Decisions in the Budget can change what families pay and what public services receive.

levels.headline: The Chancellor has very little room for his first Budget
levels.body:
John Healey is the Chancellor. He decides how much tax people pay and how the government spends its money. He will announce his first big plan, called the Budget, on 28 October. He took over the job from Rachel Reeves in July.
There is a problem. The government has set itself rules about how much it can borrow. Reports say it has only about £5bn of spare room under those rules, or even less. It is also borrowing £8.1bn more than it expected.
Mr Healey has promised not to put up income tax, employee National Insurance or VAT. These are the taxes that bring in the most money, so it is harder to find extra cash.
The Budget will cover tax, pensions, benefits and savings.
levels.why: It matters because the Budget affects taxes, pensions and benefits for millions of people.

levels.headline: A tight Budget is coming on 28 October
levels.body:
The Chancellor is the person in charge of the country's money. He is called John Healey. On 28 October he will tell everyone his plans for taxes and spending. This is called the Budget. It is the first one he has done, because he started the job in July.
The government borrows money when it spends more than it gets from taxes. It has rules about how much it can borrow. Reports say there is only a very small gap left before it breaks those rules, about £5bn or less. The government is also borrowing £8.1bn more than it planned.
Mr Healey has promised not to raise income tax, National Insurance for workers, or VAT. That makes things harder.
levels.why: It matters because the choices he makes could change what you and your family pay.

levels.headline: The government is short of spare money
levels.body:
The Chancellor is the person who looks after the government's money. This one is called John Healey. On 28 October he will share his plans for taxes and spending. This is called the Budget.
The government borrows money when it spends more than it earns from taxes. It has rules to stop it borrowing too much. People say there is very little room left under those rules. It is about £5bn or less. The government is also borrowing £8.1bn more than it planned.
Mr Healey has promised not to make three big taxes bigger. They are income tax, the National Insurance paid by workers, and VAT, which is added to many things we buy. That makes the job harder.
The Budget could change things like pensions, benefits and savings.
levels.why: It matters because the plan decides how much tax people pay and how much the government can spend.

levels.headline: Why the government needs to be careful with money
levels.body:
Think about a family that has a rule: we will not borrow more than a certain amount. This month, the family finds it has spent more than it planned. Now it has to decide what to do.
The government is a bit like that. The person in charge of its money is called the Chancellor. He is John Healey. On 28 October he will explain his plan for the next year. It is called the Budget.
The government has very little spare room under its borrowing rules. That is about £5bn or less. It is also borrowing £8.1bn more than it expected.
Mr Healey has promised not to raise three big taxes. That makes it tricky to find the money he needs.
levels.why: It matters because it affects how much money the government has for things like schools and hospitals.

levels.headline: A grown-up with a tricky sums problem
levels.body:
A grown-up called John Healey has a tricky job. He looks after the government's money, like a very big pocket money jar for the whole country. On 28 October he will tell everyone how he plans to use it. This is called the Budget.
Here is the problem. The government has a rule about how much it may borrow. Borrowing means taking money now and paying it back later. There is not much room left before it breaks the rule. The government has also borrowed more than it expected.
Mr Healey has promised not to ask for more money in three big ways. They are income tax, a tax on wages called National Insurance, and a tax called VAT that is added to things we buy.
So he must find clever ways to make the sums work.
levels.why: It matters because it decides how the country spends its money.

levels.headline: Counting the pocket money
levels.body:
Imagine your class has a jar of pocket money to pay for a party. The teacher, who looks after the jar, says you can only spend up to a limit. But the party is going to cost more than expected, and there is hardly any spare room.
This is a bit like the Chancellor's problem. The Chancellor looks after the country's money. His name is John Healey. On 28 October he will say how the country will get and spend its money. That is called the Budget.
There is very little spare room under the rules, only about £5bn. The country has also borrowed more than planned.
He has promised not to ask people for more money through three big taxes. So he will have to think hard.
levels.why: It matters because the Chancellor's choices affect families and schools across the country.

headline: Badenoch rows back on 'Iron Dome' comparison for £10bn Britannia Shield pledge

terms.meaning: Systems that detect and shoot down incoming missiles, drones and aircraft.
A missile designed to destroy another missile or drone in flight.
A public promise to do something if you win power.

levels.headline: Badenoch rows back on 'Iron Dome' comparison for £10bn Britannia Shield pledge
levels.body:
Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, has said the party's proposed £10bn missile and drone defence system, the Britannia Shield, would not be a British version of Israel's Iron Dome.
The Conservatives announced at their conference in Birmingham that they would invest up to £10bn over 10 years, identified as £1bn a year, in an integrated air and missile defence system. It would combine radar, command and control systems to detect incoming strikes with interceptor missiles and counter-drone capabilities. Mr Badenoch warned that the threat is here.
Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, she said the system is different from the Iron Dome because the threats facing the UK are different, but said the country does not currently have this sort of capability.
The earlier comparison with the Iron Dome, which Israel uses against short-range rockets, had been widely used in coverage of the announcement.
levels.why: Defence spending and national security are central issues for voters, and the plan tests how the Conservatives would pay for their promises.

levels.headline: Badenoch says £10bn Britannia Shield is not a British Iron Dome
levels.body:
Kemi Badenoch has stepped back from comparing her party's £10bn Britannia Shield defence plan to Israel's Iron Dome.
The Conservatives announced at their Birmingham conference that they would spend up to £10bn over 10 years, or £1bn a year, on an integrated air and missile defence system. It would include radar and command and control systems to spot incoming strikes, interceptor missiles and tools to counter drones.
On BBC Radio 4's Today programme, the Conservative leader said the system differs from the Iron Dome because the threats the UK faces are different. She argued, however, that Britain does not have this kind of capability at the moment.
The announcement came with a warning from Mr Badenoch that the threat is here.
The pledge is likely to prompt questions about cost, delivery and where the money would come from.
levels.why: Voters will weigh up whether the promise is realistic and affordable.

levels.headline: Badenoch: our £10bn missile shield is not a copy of Israel's Iron Dome
levels.body:
Kemi Badenoch has said the Conservatives' £10bn Britannia Shield would not be a British copy of Israel's Iron Dome, after the plan was widely described that way.
At the party's conference in Birmingham, the Conservatives promised to spend up to £10bn over 10 years, which works out at £1bn a year. The money would pay for radar and control systems that detect incoming attacks, missiles that shoot them down and equipment to stop drones.
Speaking on BBC Radio 4, Ms Badenoch said the threats facing the UK are different from those facing Israel. She added that the UK does not currently have this sort of protection.
The Iron Dome is the Israeli system used to shoot down short-range rockets.
She warned that the threat to Britain is here, but critics are likely to ask how the plan would be paid for.
levels.why: The plan shows how security concerns are shaping party promises.

levels.headline: Tories scale back 'Iron Dome' talk on £10bn Britannia Shield
levels.body:
Kemi Badenoch has said the Conservatives' planned £10bn Britannia Shield would not be a British version of Israel's Iron Dome.
The party announced the plan at its conference in Birmingham. It would spend up to £10bn over 10 years on a system to detect and stop missiles and drones, with radar, command centres and interceptor missiles. That is £1bn a year.
On BBC Radio 4's Today programme, the Conservative leader said it is different because Britain faces different threats. But she said the UK does not currently have this kind of defence and that the threat is already here.
The Iron Dome is the Israeli system that shoots down short-range rockets. Many reports had used the comparison when the plan was first announced.
Opponents are expected to question the cost and how soon it could be built.
levels.why: It is about how safe the country is and how much the government is willing to spend on defence.

levels.headline: Badenoch says the new missile shield is not like Israel's Iron Dome
levels.body:
Kemi Badenoch, who leads the Conservatives, has said her party's new defence plan is not a copy of Israel's Iron Dome.
The plan is called the Britannia Shield. At the party's conference in Birmingham, the Conservatives said they would spend up to £10bn over 10 years on it. That is £1bn a year. The system would use radar to spot missiles and drones coming towards the UK. It would also have missiles that shoot them down.
On BBC Radio 4, Ms Badenoch said the threats facing Britain are different from the ones Israel faces. She said Britain does not have this kind of protection now, and that the threat is here.
The Iron Dome is the system Israel uses to stop short-range rockets.
Other parties may ask how the Conservatives would pay for it.
levels.why: It matters because defending the country costs a lot of money, and parties must explain how they would pay.

levels.headline: Conservatives promise £10bn to protect the UK from missiles and drones
levels.body:
The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, has made a big promise. Her party says it would spend up to £10bn over 10 years to protect the UK from missiles and drones. That is £1bn a year.
The plan is called the Britannia Shield. It would use radar to spot dangerous missiles or drones. Then special missiles would stop them before they land.
When the plan was first announced, many people said it was like Israel's Iron Dome. That is a system that shoots down rockets. Ms Badenoch has now said it is not the same. She said the UK faces different dangers. She also said the UK does not have this kind of protection today.
She spoke about it on BBC Radio 4. She announced the plan at her party's conference in Birmingham.
levels.why: It matters because it shows how much the Conservatives want to spend on defence.

levels.headline: The Conservatives want a shield against missiles and drones

She told the BBC about the plan after the party's conference in Birmingham.

levels.headline: A shield in the sky

Imagine a big invisible umbrella over the whole country. If something dangerous flew towards it, the umbrella would stop it before it landed. A party called the Conservatives wants to build something like that.
They call it the Britannia Shield. It would use radar, which is like very good eyes, to spot dangerous missiles and drones. Then it would use other missiles to stop them in the sky.
Building it would cost £10bn over 10 years. That is a huge amount, like everyone in the school playground giving up their pocket money for ten years.
The leader of the party is Kemi Badenoch. Some people said the idea was like the Iron Dome in Israel. She said it is not the same, because the dangers here are different.

headline: UK inflation rises to 3.1% as energy price cap heads higher

terms.meaning: The rate at which prices in the shops and for services rise over time.
Inflation leaving out volatile items such as food and energy.
A limit on the price per unit of gas and electricity that suppliers can charge.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.1% as energy price cap heads higher
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.1% in the 12 months to August 2026, up from 2.9% in July, according to the latest figures.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile items such as food and energy, was 2.6%, and the CPIH measure, which includes housing costs, was 3.3%. The rise comes as the Iran war continues to push up energy prices.
The energy price cap for a typical household's gas and electricity use rose to £1,723 for October to December, from £1,663 in the previous quarter. Forecasters expect another increase in January 2027. E.ON's September forecast is £2,065, while EDF's forecast on 28 September is £2,076.
The Bank of England's target is 2%, and it has said that energy prices remain volatile because of the Middle East conflict and could push inflation higher still.
levels.why: Rising prices and bills squeeze household budgets and shape decisions on interest rates.

levels.headline: Inflation up to 3.1% with bigger energy bills expected in January
levels.body:
Consumer price inflation in the UK increased to 3.1% in the year to August 2026, from 2.9% in July.
Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, was 2.6%. CPIH, a measure including housing costs, stood at 3.3%. Higher energy costs linked to the war involving Iran are a key pressure.
The Ofgem price cap for a typical household has risen to £1,723 for the October to December quarter, up from £1,663 for July to September. Forecasts point to a further rise in January 2027, with E.ON predicting £2,065 and EDF £2,076.
Inflation is above the Bank of England's 2% target, and the Bank has said energy markets remain volatile because of the conflict in the Middle East.
levels.why: Higher bills reduce what households can spend and make it harder for the Bank of England to cut interest rates.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster, and energy bills are set to go up again
levels.body:
UK inflation rose to 3.1% in the year to August 2026, up from 2.9% the month before.
Core inflation, which leaves out food and energy because they move around a lot, was 2.6%. Another measure, CPIH, which includes housing costs, was 3.3%. Energy costs have been pushed up by the war involving Iran.
The energy price cap, which limits what suppliers can charge per unit of gas and electricity, rose to £1,723 for a typical household for October to December. It was £1,663 for the previous three months. Forecasters expect it to go up again in January 2027, to between £2,065 and £2,076.
The Bank of England wants inflation at 2%, so 3.1% is well above its target.
levels.why: Higher bills hit family budgets, and inflation influences interest rates and mortgages.

levels.headline: Inflation edges up to 3.1% and winter energy bills look set to rise
levels.body:
Inflation in the UK rose to 3.1% in the year to August, up from 2.9% in July.
Core inflation, which does not include food and energy prices, was 2.6%. A wider measure that includes housing costs was 3.3%. The war involving Iran is making energy more expensive.
A typical household's energy price cap is now £1,723 for October to December, up from £1,663. Forecasters predict a bigger jump in January 2027, to about £2,065 according to E.ON and £2,076 according to EDF.
The Bank of England aims for inflation of 2%. It says energy prices are still unpredictable because of the conflict in the Middle East, and that they could push inflation up further.
levels.why: It affects how much people pay for gas, electricity and food, and how much they can save.

levels.headline: Prices are going up faster, and gas and electricity bills will rise
levels.body:
Inflation is how fast prices go up. In the year to August 2026, UK prices rose by 3.1%. In July it was 2.9%, so things are getting more expensive a little faster.
Some prices, such as food and energy, jump around a lot. Without them, the rate was 2.6%. A different measure that includes housing costs was 3.3%. Energy is dearer partly because of the war involving Iran.
There is a limit on what energy firms can charge, called the price cap. For a typical home it is now £1,723 for October to December. Last time it was £1,663. Experts think it will rise again in January 2027, to over £2,000.
The Bank of England wants inflation to be 2%.
levels.why: It matters because rising prices make everyday life more expensive.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster, and bills will rise again
levels.body:
Inflation is the name for prices going up over time. The latest figures show that UK prices in August were 3.1% higher than a year earlier. In July the figure was 2.9%, so prices are climbing a little faster. The Bank of England wants prices to rise by only 2% a year.
Energy is a big reason. There is a war involving Iran, and it has made energy dearer. The energy price cap is a limit on what firms can charge for gas and electricity. For a typical home it is now £1,723 for October to December, up from £1,663 for the three months before.
Experts expect the cap to go up again in January 2027, to about £2,065 to £2,076. That would make heating and lighting a home cost a lot more in the winter.
levels.why: It matters because higher prices and bills leave families with less money to spend.

levels.headline: Prices are rising a little faster, and energy bills will go up
levels.body:
Inflation means prices going up over time. The latest figures show UK prices were 3.1% higher in August than a year before. In July the figure was 2.9%.
The country wants prices to rise by only 2% a year. So 3.1% is higher than hoped. Part of the reason is the price of energy. There is a war involving Iran, and that has made energy dearer.
Energy companies can only charge up to a set limit, called the price cap. For a normal home, the limit is now £1,723 a year for October to December. It was £1,663 before. People who study this think it will go up again in January 2027, to over £2,000.
That means heating and lighting a home will cost more.
levels.why: It matters because families may have less money left for other things.

levels.headline: Things cost a bit more, and heating bills will rise
levels.body:
When prices go up, we call it inflation. If a sweet cost 100p last year and 103p now, that is about 3% inflation. In the UK, prices in August were 3.1% higher than a year before. In July it was 2.9%.
The government would like prices to go up by only 2% a year. So things are rising faster than hoped. One reason is that energy has become more expensive. There is a war involving Iran, and that has made oil and gas cost more.
There is a limit on what firms can charge for gas and electricity at home. It is called the price cap. It is now £1,723 for a typical home for three months. People expect it to go up again in January 2027, to over £2,000.
That can make families worry.
levels.why: It matters because more expensive bills mean families have less money for other things.

levels.headline: Why things cost more than before
levels.body:
Prices change over time. Something that cost £1 last year might cost a bit more now. When lots of prices go up together, that is called inflation.
In the UK, prices in August were 3.1% higher than a year earlier. That means a £100 shopping trip would now cost about £103. People want prices to go up by only 2%, so 3.1% is more than hoped.
One reason is energy, which means the gas and electricity used to heat and light homes. There is a war involving Iran, and it has made energy cost more. In January 2027, bills for a typical home are expected to go up again.
That can make it harder for families to pay for everything they need.
levels.why: It matters because when things cost more, families can buy less.

levels.headline: Why your sweets cost more
levels.body:
Imagine your favourite sweets cost 100p last year. This year they cost 103p. That small rise is a bit like what is happening to lots of prices in the UK. People call it inflation.
Grown-ups want prices to rise slowly, like 2p on a 100p sweet. Now it is a little faster than that. One reason is that energy has become more expensive. Energy is what heats homes and turns on the lights. There is a war far away that has made it cost more.
The companies that sell it can only charge up to a limit. That limit is about to go up again in January. It means families will pay more to keep warm.
So grown-ups are watching prices carefully.
levels.why: It matters because when everything costs a bit more, your family has less spare money.

headline: Bank of England holds rates at 3.75% for sixth meeting in a row

terms.meaning: The Bank of England's main interest rate, which influences mortgage and savings rates.
The group of nine experts who set Bank Rate.
The 2% yearly rise in prices that the Bank of England aims for.

levels.headline: Bank of England holds rates at 3.75% for sixth meeting in a row
levels.body:
The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee voted six to three on 17 September to keep Bank Rate at 3.75%, the sixth consecutive meeting at which rates have been left unchanged.
Inflation is 3.1%, above the Bank's 2% target, and the Bank has said that energy prices remain volatile because of the conflict in the Middle East. Energy costs have risen further recently, which means inflation is expected to rise from its current level.
The longer energy prices stay high, the greater the risk that higher inflation becomes persistent, which is shaping the Bank's cautious approach to any change in rates.
Bank Rate influences what banks charge on mortgages and loans and what they pay on savings. Holding it steady means borrowers have not seen the relief that lower rates would bring, while savers keep the current returns.
levels.why: Interest rates affect mortgages, loans and savings for millions of households.

levels.headline: Bank holds Bank Rate at 3.75% as energy-driven inflation worries persist
levels.body:
The Bank of England kept Bank Rate at 3.75% on 17 September. The Monetary Policy Committee voted six to three, and it was the sixth meeting in a row without a change.
Inflation, at 3.1%, is above the Bank's 2% target. The Bank has pointed to volatile energy prices caused by the conflict in the Middle East, and says inflation will rise from its present level because energy costs have gone up again.
The longer energy prices remain high, the greater the risk of persistent inflation, and that is why the Bank is being careful.
Bank Rate guides the cost of mortgages and loans and the interest paid on savings, so a long hold means little change for many households.
levels.why: The Bank is trying to balance higher energy-driven prices against a weaker economy.

levels.headline: Interest rates stay at 3.75% for the sixth time in a row
levels.body:
The Bank of England decided on 17 September to keep its main interest rate, Bank Rate, at 3.75%. It is the sixth meeting in a row where rates did not change. Six members of the Monetary Policy Committee voted to hold, and three voted differently.
Inflation is now 3.1%, above the Bank's 2% target. Energy prices are going up because of the conflict in the Middle East, so the Bank expects inflation to rise further.
If energy stays expensive for a long time, higher prices could become a lasting problem. That is why the Bank is being careful about changing rates.
Bank Rate affects the cost of mortgages and loans and the interest you earn on savings.
levels.why: It affects what people pay on mortgages and earn on savings.

levels.headline: Bank of England leaves interest rates at 3.75%
levels.body:
The Bank of England has kept its main interest rate at 3.75%. The decision was made on 17 September by a group of experts called the Monetary Policy Committee. Six voted to keep the rate where it is, and three voted for something different. This was the sixth meeting in a row with no change.
Prices are going up faster than the Bank wants. Inflation is 3.1%, and the Bank aims for 2%. Energy costs are rising because of the conflict in the Middle East, so inflation is expected to go higher.
The Bank worries that if energy stays expensive for a long time, high inflation could stick around. So it is being careful.
The rate affects what people pay on mortgages and loans and earn on savings.
levels.why: It matters because the rate sets how expensive it is to borrow money.

levels.headline: Interest rates are staying the same for now
levels.body:
The Bank of England is the bank that looks after the UK's money. It sets an interest rate called Bank Rate. This rate affects how much people pay on loans and mortgages and how much they earn on savings. It is now 3.75%.
On 17 September, a group of experts at the Bank voted on whether to change it. Six wanted to keep it the same. Three wanted something different. It is the sixth time in a row that the rate has stayed the same.
The Bank wants prices to go up by only 2% a year. Now they are going up by 3.1%. Energy is more expensive because of the conflict in the Middle East, so prices may rise more.
The Bank is waiting to see what happens before it changes anything.
levels.why: It matters because the rate changes how much families pay to borrow money.

levels.headline: The Bank of England keeps interest rates the same
levels.body:
The Bank of England has a job: to stop prices rising too fast. Its main tool is an interest rate called Bank Rate, which affects how much people pay on loans and mortgages and how much they earn on savings. It is now 3.75%.
On 17 September, a group of nine experts called the Monetary Policy Committee voted on whether to change it. Six voted to keep it the same and three voted for something else. It is the sixth meeting in a row with no change.
The Bank wants prices to rise by 2% a year, but inflation is now 3.1%. Energy is getting more expensive because of the conflict in the Middle East, so prices could go up further. If that lasts a long time, high prices could become hard to bring down.
So the Bank is being careful.
levels.why: It matters because the rate affects families who borrow money or have savings.

levels.headline: Why the Bank of England has left interest rates alone
levels.body:
The Bank of England has a job. It tries to keep prices from rising too fast. Its main tool is an interest rate called Bank Rate. When the rate is high, borrowing money costs more and saving pays more. It is now 3.75%.
On 17 September, nine experts met to decide whether to change it. Six voted to leave it alone and three voted for something different. This is the sixth time in a row it has stayed the same.
Prices are going up by 3.1% a year. The Bank wants 2%. One reason is that energy is getting more expensive because of conflict in the Middle East. The Bank thinks prices could go up more.
So it is staying careful.
levels.why: It matters because the rate affects families with mortgages and savings.

levels.headline: The interest rate is not changing
levels.body:
Banks charge interest when they lend money. Interest is a bit extra that you pay back. The Bank of England sets a main rate that guides how much interest everyone pays. It is called Bank Rate. It is 3.75% now.
On 17 September, nine experts at the Bank voted on whether to change it. Six said keep it. Three said something else. It has now stayed the same six times in a row.
The experts want prices to go up slowly, by 2% each year. But prices are going up by 3.1%. Energy costs more because of conflict far away, so prices might go up more.
So the experts decided to wait.
levels.why: It matters because the rate affects how much people pay when they borrow.

levels.headline: Waiting and watching
levels.body:
Some grown-ups borrow money to buy a house. They pay back more than they borrowed. That extra is called interest. A big bank called the Bank of England sets a rate that helps decide how much interest people pay. It is 3.75%.
The bank has a group of experts. On 17 September they voted on whether to change the rate. Six voted to keep it. Three voted for something else. This is the sixth time in a row it has not changed.
The experts want prices to go up slowly. Right now they are going up faster than they like. Energy costs more, because of a faraway conflict.
So the experts decided to wait and see.
levels.why: It matters because it affects how much money families have to pay back.

levels.headline: The grown-ups who keep prices steady
levels.body:
Imagine a school tuck shop. The prices should only go up a tiny bit each year. If they rise too fast, nobody can afford a snack.
There is a bank in the UK that tries to stop prices rising too fast. It is called the Bank of England. It has a special button, like a volume control, called the interest rate. It is at 3.75%. Turning it up makes borrowing money cost more. Turning it down makes it cost less.
On 17 September, a group of nine experts voted on whether to move it. Six said no. Three said something else. They have left it in the same place six times in a row.
Prices are rising a bit fast, so they are being careful.
levels.why: It matters because families who borrow or save are affected by the rate.

headline: UK unemployment holds at 4.9% as payrolls fall and vacancies hit five-year low

terms.meaning: The share of people who want a job and are looking for one but cannot find work.
People counted as being paid by employers through the tax system.
Job openings that employers are trying to fill.

levels.headline: UK unemployment holds at 4.9% as payrolls fall and vacancies hit five-year low
levels.body:
The UK unemployment rate was 4.9% in the three months to July 2026, according to the Office for National Statistics, better than the 5.0% economists had forecast but above the 4.7% of a year earlier.
About 1.78 million people aged 16 and over were unemployed, an increase of 83,000 over the year.
There were warning signs elsewhere in the figures. The number of payrolled employees fell by 26,000 in August 2026, more than five times the fall that economists had expected. Vacancies dropped to 702,000 in the three months to August, the lowest level since 2021 outside the pandemic period.
The figures were published on 15 September. They give the Bank of England a mixed picture, as a weaker jobs market could ease pressure on wages and prices, while energy costs are pushing inflation up.
levels.why: A weakening jobs market affects wages, household confidence and the Bank of England's decisions on interest rates.

levels.headline: Unemployment steady at 4.9%, but jobs market shows signs of weakening
levels.body:
Unemployment in the UK was 4.9% in the three months to July 2026, the ONS reported. That was lower than the 5.0% forecast, but higher than the 4.7% recorded a year earlier.
In total 1.78 million people aged 16 and over were out of work, up by 83,000 in a year.
Other numbers were weaker. Payrolled employment fell by 26,000 in August, over five times the drop economists had predicted. Job vacancies fell to 702,000 in the three months to August, the lowest since 2021 apart from during the pandemic.
The figures, released on 15 September, leave the Bank of England weighing a softer labour market against inflation driven by energy prices.
levels.why: Fewer jobs and vacancies can mean less bargaining power for workers and slower wage growth.

levels.headline: Unemployment stays at 4.9%, but fewer jobs are being advertised
levels.body:
The UK unemployment rate was 4.9% in the three months to July 2026, the ONS said. That was slightly better than the 5.0% experts expected, but higher than 4.7% a year ago.
About 1.78 million people were unemployed, which is 83,000 more than a year earlier.
Other figures looked worse. The number of employees on company payrolls fell by 26,000 in August, much more than economists had expected. Vacancies, meaning jobs employers are trying to fill, fell to 702,000, the lowest since 2021 apart from the pandemic.
The figures came out on 15 September. They show the jobs market cooling just as higher energy prices push up the cost of living.
levels.why: It affects people looking for work and could influence interest rates.

levels.headline: Unemployment holds at 4.9% but payrolls fall and vacancies drop
levels.body:
Unemployment in the UK was 4.9% in the three months to July 2026. That was a bit better than the 5.0% that economists had forecast, but it is up from 4.7% a year earlier.
About 1.78 million people did not have a job but wanted one, which is 83,000 more than a year ago.
Other numbers were less positive. The number of people on employers' payrolls fell by 26,000 in August. That was a much bigger fall than expected. Job vacancies dropped to 702,000, the lowest since 2021, not counting the pandemic.
The Office for National Statistics published the figures on 15 September. The weaker jobs market is happening at the same time as energy costs are pushing prices up.
levels.why: It matters because fewer jobs make it harder for people to find work or get pay rises.

levels.headline: About one in twenty people looking for work cannot find a job
levels.body:
The latest official figures show the UK unemployment rate is 4.9%. That means nearly one in twenty people who want a job cannot find one. A year ago it was 4.7%. About 1.78 million people are out of work, which is 83,000 more than last year.
There are other signs that finding work is getting harder. In August, the number of people being paid by companies fell by 26,000. Economists had expected a much smaller fall. The number of job vacancies also dropped, to 702,000. That is the lowest since 2021, apart from during the pandemic.
The Office for National Statistics shared the figures on 15 September.
When fewer jobs are on offer, it can be harder for workers to ask for pay rises.
levels.why: It matters because jobs and pay affect how families pay their bills.

levels.headline: Fewer jobs are being offered across the UK
levels.body:
The UK unemployment rate is 4.9%, according to the latest official figures. That means nearly one in twenty people who want a job cannot find one. A year ago the rate was 4.7%. About 1.78 million people are out of work, 83,000 more than a year earlier.
There are other signs that the jobs market is cooling. The number of people being paid by employers fell by 26,000 in August, a much bigger fall than experts had expected. Job vacancies, which are jobs employers are trying to fill, dropped to 702,000. That is the lowest level since 2021, apart from during the pandemic.
The figures were published by the Office for National Statistics on 15 September. When there are fewer jobs, it can be harder for workers to ask for pay rises.
levels.why: It matters because jobs and pay decide how well families can afford their bills.

levels.headline: Fewer jobs are on offer in the UK
levels.body:
The Office for National Statistics counts how many people have jobs. Its latest report shows 4.9% of people who want to work could not find a job. That is nearly one in twenty. A year ago it was 4.7%, so it has gone up a little. About 1.78 million people are without a job.
Companies also cut the number of people on their payrolls by 26,000 in August. That was more than experts had expected. And fewer jobs are being advertised. There are now 702,000 vacancies, which is the lowest number since 2021, not counting the time of the pandemic.
The figures came out on 15 September.
When jobs are harder to find, workers may find it harder to get a pay rise.
levels.why: It matters because people need jobs to pay for food, homes and bills.

levels.headline: Finding a job is getting harder
levels.body:
A job is work you do to get paid. The government counts how many people want a job and cannot get one. This is the unemployment rate. It is now 4.9%. That is about one person in every twenty who wants to work. A year ago it was a bit lower.
Companies are also hiring fewer people. In August, 26,000 fewer people were being paid by companies than the month before. And there are fewer adverts for jobs. There are 702,000 jobs on offer. That is the lowest number in a long time.
The Office for National Statistics, which counts these things, shared the numbers on 15 September.
When it is hard to find work, families can struggle to pay for things they need.
levels.why: It matters because people need jobs to take care of their families.

levels.headline: Fewer jobs for grown-ups
levels.body:
Most grown-ups go to work to earn money. They use the money to pay for food, clothes and the place they live. But sometimes it is hard to find a job.
The latest count shows that about one in every twenty grown-ups who want a job cannot find one. A number is used to show this. It is 4.9%. Last year it was a little smaller.
Less work is on offer, too. In August, 26,000 fewer people were being paid by companies. Also, there are fewer adverts for new jobs, only 702,000. That is the lowest in a long time.
A group called the Office for National Statistics counts all of this and told us on 15 September.
levels.why: It matters because when it is hard to find a job, a family has less money.

levels.headline: When there are fewer jobs
levels.body:
Imagine a school fair with lots of stalls that need helpers. Last year there were plenty of stalls looking for helpers. This year, there are fewer stalls, and more children are waiting for a turn to help.
That is a bit like the jobs market in the UK. Counting shows that about one in every twenty grown-ups who want a job cannot find one. Companies are also hiring fewer people. The number of job adverts is the lowest in a long time.
The group that counts these things is called the Office for National Statistics. It told us on 15 September.
When it is hard to find a job, families can find it harder to buy what they need.
levels.why: It matters because having a job helps families pay for the things they need.

headline: UK economy grows 0.4% in three months to July, eighth straight quarterly rise

terms.meaning: Gross domestic product, the total value of goods and services produced in the economy.
Businesses that sell services, such as shops, banks, restaurants and healthcare.
Output from factories, mining, energy and water supply.

levels.headline: UK economy grows 0.4% in three months to July, eighth straight quarterly rise
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.4% in the three months to July 2026, following growth of 0.4% in the three months to June, the Office for National Statistics reported. It was the eighth consecutive three-month-on-three-month rise.
Monthly GDP grew by 0.4% in July, after growth of 0.3% in June and no growth in May. The figure beat expectations of no growth.
The services sector, which grew by 0.6%, was the main driver of the expansion. Production fell by 0.5% and construction fell by 0.5% over the three months.
The figures suggest the economy has kept growing despite higher energy prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East, although unemployment has risen and business confidence has weakened. The ONS publishes monthly estimates of GDP, which measures the total value of what the economy produces.
levels.why: Steady growth supports jobs and tax revenues, but it is uneven across sectors.

levels.headline: UK GDP up 0.4% in the three months to July, led by services
levels.body:
UK GDP rose by 0.4% in the three months to July 2026, the same rate as in the three months to June. The ONS said it was the eighth consecutive three-month growth period.
On a monthly basis, GDP grew 0.4% in July, following 0.3% in June and zero in May. Economists had expected no growth for July.
Services, up 0.6%, were the main source of growth. Production and construction each fell by 0.5%.
The economy has therefore kept expanding despite the pressure from higher energy costs linked to the Middle East conflict. At the same time, unemployment has risen and business confidence has weakened, so the picture is mixed.
levels.why: It shows the economy is more resilient than expected, but not every part of it is doing well.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew 0.4% over three months to July
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.4% in the three months to July 2026. That is the same as the growth in the three months to June, and the eighth time in a row that the economy has grown over a three-month period, the ONS said.
Looking at July alone, the economy grew by 0.4%. In June it grew by 0.3%, and in May it did not grow. Experts had expected no growth in July.
Most of the growth came from services such as shops, restaurants, banks and healthcare, which grew by 0.6%. Production, such as factory output, and construction both shrank by 0.5%.
The economy is still growing despite higher energy prices, though business confidence has weakened.
levels.why: Growth helps create jobs and raise money for public services.

levels.headline: UK economy keeps growing, with a 0.4% rise to July
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.4% in the three months to July 2026, the same as the period before. It is the eighth three-month period in a row with growth, according to the ONS.
In July itself, the economy grew by 0.4%. June's growth was 0.3% and there was no growth in May. Economists had predicted no growth in July.
The services sector, which includes shops, pubs, banks and hospitals, grew by 0.6% and did most of the work. Factories and other production fell by 0.5%, and construction also fell by 0.5%.
The economy has held up despite higher energy prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
levels.why: A growing economy usually means more jobs and more money for public services.

levels.headline: The UK economy is still growing
levels.body:
The economy is everything people make and sell in the country, from haircuts to cars. Experts measure it with a number called GDP. The latest figures show the UK economy grew by 0.4% in the three months to July. That is the eighth time in a row it has grown over a three-month period.
Just looking at July, it grew by 0.4% as well. Experts had thought it would not grow at all.
Most growth came from services, which means jobs like shops, restaurants and banks. Factories and building work both shrank.
The economy kept growing even though energy has become more expensive. That is partly because of the war involving Iran.
levels.why: It matters because a growing economy helps create jobs.

levels.headline: The UK economy has grown again
levels.body:
The economy is everything that people in the country make, sell and do to earn money, from haircuts to cars. Experts measure it with a number called GDP. The latest figures show the UK economy grew by 0.4% in the three months to July. That is the eighth three-month period in a row in which it has grown.
Just looking at July, it grew by 0.4%, too. Experts had thought it would not grow at all, so it was a pleasant surprise.
Most of the growth came from services, such as shops, banks and restaurants, which grew by 0.6%. Factories and building work both made less than before.
The economy kept growing even though energy has become more expensive because of the war involving Iran.
levels.why: It matters because a growing economy helps to create jobs and raise money for public services.

levels.headline: Britain's economy grew again
levels.body:
The economy is all the things people in the country make, sell and do to earn money. A number called GDP measures it. The Office for National Statistics counts it. It said that the UK economy grew by 0.4% in the three months to July. It has now grown for eight three-month periods in a row.
In July alone, it grew by 0.4% too. Experts thought it would stay the same, so this was a nice surprise.
The biggest growth came from services. These are things like shops, cafes, banks and hospitals. But factories and building work made less than before.
The economy kept growing even though energy costs more now.
levels.why: It matters because when the economy grows, there are more jobs and more money to share.

levels.headline: The country's money machine is still growing
levels.body:
The economy is like a big machine that makes money. It makes it when people buy and sell things, such as food, clothes and haircuts. A number called GDP shows how big the machine is.
The latest report says the UK economy grew by 0.4% in the three months to July. That is a small amount, but it is the eighth time in a row it has grown over three months.
In July alone it grew by 0.4%. Experts thought it would stay the same.
Most of the growth came from services like shops and cafes. But factories made less, and so did builders.
It has grown even though energy costs more because of a war far away.
levels.why: It matters because it helps more people to have jobs.

levels.headline: Is the country getting richer?
levels.body:
Every day, people in the UK make things and do jobs for each other. They bake bread, fix cars, teach children and look after people in hospital. All of this work added up is called the economy.
The economy is measured by a number called GDP. Experts at the Office for National Statistics counted it and said it grew by 0.4% in three months to July. That is a small step up, like adding a little to a pile of coins. It has gone up eight times in a row.
The biggest growth was in services, like shops and cafes. Factories and building work went down a bit.
That is good news, even though energy has become more costly.
levels.why: It matters because a bigger economy can mean more jobs.

levels.headline: A growing pile of coins
levels.body:
Imagine a big pile of coins that belongs to the whole country. Each day, people add coins by working, baking, building and selling things. The pile is the economy.
Experts count the pile every three months. The latest count says it grew by 0.4% to July. That is only a little more, like adding a few coins, but it is the eighth time in a row it has grown.
Most of the new coins came from shops, cafes and other services. The factories and builders added fewer.
Energy has become more expensive because of a faraway war. The pile still grew, which is good news.
levels.why: It matters because when the pile grows, there can be more jobs and more to share.

levels.headline: Fifteen candidates contest Holborn and St Pancras by-election on 8 October
levels.body:
Voters in Holborn and St Pancras go to the polls on Thursday 8 October to choose a new MP in a by-election, with 15 candidates on the ballot.
The candidates include Sagal Abdi-Wali for Labour, Ewan Cameron for the Conservatives, Peter Newman for Reform UK, Zack Polanski for the Green Party, Patrick Stillman for the Liberal Democrats and George Galloway for the Workers Party. The field also includes Barmy Brunch (Official Monster Raving Loony Party), Clare Fisher (Climate Party), Tom Darwood (independent), Ketankumar Pipaliya (UK VOICE), Jonathan Silberman (Communist League), Helen Spiby-Vann (Christian Peoples Alliance) and Ben Walker (UKIP).
A by-election is held when a seat in the House of Commons becomes vacant between general elections. Such contests are often watched closely as a test of how the parties are doing nationally.
levels.why: By-elections are watched as a test of public mood between general elections.

levels.headline: Holborn and St Pancras by-election: 15 candidates stand on 8 October

People in the London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras vote on Thursday 8 October to elect a new MP, with 15 candidates standing.

levels.headline: Voters choose a new MP for Holborn and St Pancras

Voters in Holborn and St Pancras, in London, choose a new MP on Thursday 8 October. There are 15 candidates.

levels.why: It decides who represents the area in Parliament and shows how popular each party is.

levels.headline: Fifteen candidates in Holborn and St Pancras by-election
levels.body:

levels.headline: Holborn and St Pancras votes for a new MP on Thursday

People in Holborn and St Pancras in London vote on Thursday 8 October. They are choosing a new MP in a by-election. Fifteen people want the job.

levels.headline: Holborn and St Pancras chooses a new MP

People in Holborn and St Pancras, a part of London, vote on Thursday 8 October to choose a new MP. An MP is the person who speaks for an area in Parliament, the place where the country's laws are made. Fifteen people are standing.

levels.why: It matters because the winner will speak for local people in Parliament.

levels.headline: Local people choose a new MP on Thursday

On Thursday 8 October, people in part of London called Holborn and St Pancras will vote. They are choosing a new MP. An MP is a person who speaks for local people in Parliament, where laws are made.

levels.headline: A vote to pick a new MP
levels.body:
Parliament is the place where grown-ups in charge make laws for the country. Every area has a person called an MP who speaks for it there.

levels.why: It matters because local people get to choose who speaks for them.

levels.headline: Choosing someone to speak for you

Sometimes we need to choose a person to speak for us. In your class, you might vote for a school council member.

levels.why: It matters because voting gives people a say in who makes the rules.

levels.headline: Picking a team captain
levels.body:
Think about picking a captain for your team at school. Everyone who wants the job says why they would be good at it. Then everyone votes. The one with the most votes becomes the captain.
Grown-ups do something like this. In one part of London, called Holborn and St Pancras, people are voting for someone to speak for them in Parliament. Parliament is where the rules of the country are made. The person they choose is called an MP.
