The vote is on Thursday 8 October.
levels.why: It matters because voting lets everyone have a say.

headline: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan activate Mecca defence pact for first time

terms.meaning: An agreement that an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.
An Iran-backed armed group that controls much of Yemen.
Showing strength so that an enemy decides not to attack.

levels.headline: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan activate Mecca defence pact for first time
levels.body:
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have activated collective deterrence measures under the Mecca defence pact and agreed to deploy forces and military capabilities rapidly to the kingdom.
The decision, taken on Monday after an emergency meeting of the pact's committee, is the first time the alliance has been invoked since it was signed on 7 August. The committee reaffirmed solidarity in confronting attacks on Saudi Arabia and Islamic holy sites.
The move follows escalating attacks by Yemen's Houthis, an Iran-backed group. The Houthis have claimed strikes on Saudi targets, including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco refinery in Rabigh and an airbase. Saudi-backed Yemeni troops have meanwhile advanced against the Houthis.
The pact treats an armed attack on one member as an attack on all three.
levels.why: It is the first real test of a new alliance, and it widens military involvement in the region.

levels.headline: Mecca alliance invoked for first time after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
levels.body:
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have activated collective deterrence measures under the Mecca defence pact, agreeing to supply military forces and capabilities and to deploy them to the kingdom quickly.
The decision came on Monday after an emergency meeting of the pact's committee. It is the first time the alliance has been invoked since it was signed on 7 August, and the committee reaffirmed solidarity against attacks on Saudi Arabia and Islamic holy sites.
The trigger was a rise in attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, who claim to have hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco refinery in Rabigh and an airbase. Saudi-backed Yemeni troops are advancing against the Houthis.
Under the pact, an armed attack on one member counts as an attack on all.
levels.why: The test shows how far regional powers will go to defend one another, and it could deepen the conflict.

levels.headline: Three countries activate a defence pact to protect Saudi Arabia
levels.body:
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have activated their Mecca defence pact for the first time. They agreed to send military forces and equipment quickly to Saudi Arabia.
The decision was taken on Monday at an emergency meeting of the pact's committee. The pact was signed on 7 August. Its members promised to stand together against attacks on Saudi Arabia and on Islamic holy sites.
The move came after more attacks from the Houthis, an armed group in Yemen backed by Iran. The Houthis say they hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco oil refinery in Rabigh and an airbase. Meanwhile, Yemeni troops backed by Saudi Arabia have been advancing against the Houthis.
The pact says an attack on one member is an attack on all three.
levels.why: It matters because the war in the Middle East could spread, and this changes who is involved.

levels.headline: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan act on their joint defence agreement
levels.body:
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have used their Mecca defence pact for the first time. They said they would send soldiers and equipment to Saudi Arabia quickly.
They decided this on Monday at an emergency meeting. The three countries signed the pact on 7 August. They promised to stand together if one of them, or Islamic holy sites, are attacked.
The decision followed more attacks by the Houthis, a group in Yemen that is backed by Iran. The Houthis say they hit an airport in Riyadh, an oil refinery in Rabigh and an airbase. Troops in Yemen backed by Saudi Arabia have been moving forward against the Houthis.
In the pact, an attack on one country counts as an attack on all three.
levels.why: It matters because it shows countries joining together as fighting grows in the region.

levels.headline: Three countries promise to defend each other
levels.body:
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have an agreement to defend each other. It is called the Mecca defence pact, and they signed it on 7 August. On Monday they used it for the first time.
They agreed to send soldiers and equipment to Saudi Arabia quickly. This is because of attacks by the Houthis. The Houthis are an armed group in Yemen, the country next to Saudi Arabia, and Iran supports them. The Houthis say they attacked an airport in Riyadh, an oil refinery and an airbase.
The three countries met in an emergency meeting and said they would stand together. The pact says an attack on one is an attack on all.
Yemeni soldiers backed by Saudi Arabia are fighting the Houthis, too.
levels.why: It matters because it could make the fighting in the region bigger.

levels.headline: Three countries use their promise to defend each other
levels.body:
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have a promise to defend each other. It is called the Mecca defence pact, and they signed it on 7 August. This week, on Monday, they used it for the first time.
They did it because of attacks by the Houthis, an armed group in Yemen that is backed by Iran. The Houthis say they hit an airport in Riyadh, an oil refinery in Rabigh and an airbase in Saudi Arabia. Yemeni soldiers backed by Saudi Arabia are also fighting the Houthis.
The three countries held an emergency meeting and agreed to send soldiers and equipment to Saudi Arabia quickly. Under the pact, an attack on one of them counts as an attack on all three. They also said they would stand together to protect Islamic holy sites.
levels.why: It matters because more countries joining in could make the conflict in the region bigger.

levels.headline: Friends agree to help each other
levels.body:
Three countries have a promise to help each other if they are attacked. They are Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan. The promise is called the Mecca defence pact. They made it on 7 August.
On Monday, they used it for the first time. This happened because a group called the Houthis, in Yemen, attacked places in Saudi Arabia. The Houthis are supported by Iran. They say they hit an airport in the city of Riyadh, an oil refinery and an airbase.
So the three countries held an emergency meeting. They agreed to send soldiers and equipment to Saudi Arabia quickly. In their promise, an attack on one country is an attack on all three.
Soldiers in Yemen are fighting the Houthis, too.
levels.why: It matters because it means more countries could become involved in the fighting.

levels.headline: Three countries stand together
levels.body:
Some countries make promises to protect each other. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan made one on 7 August. It is called the Mecca defence pact. If someone attacks one of them, it is like attacking all three.
On Monday, they used the promise for the first time. A group in Yemen called the Houthis has been attacking places in Saudi Arabia. The Houthis say they hit an airport and an oil refinery. Iran backs the Houthis.
The three countries met and agreed to send soldiers and equipment to Saudi Arabia quickly. They want to show that they are strong together, so that nobody attacks again.
Soldiers in Yemen who are backed by Saudi Arabia are fighting the Houthis, too.
levels.why: It matters because more countries could get involved in the fighting.

levels.headline: Teaming up to stay safe
levels.body:
Think about a group of friends in the playground who promise to look after each other. If someone picks on one of them, all of them step in. That is called a team promise.
Three countries have made a team promise like this. They are Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan. They made it on 7 August. This week, they used it for the first time.
Some people from Yemen, called the Houthis, have been attacking Saudi Arabia. The Houthis say they hit an airport and an oil refinery. So the three countries agreed to send soldiers and equipment to Saudi Arabia, to keep it safe.
It is meant to make others think twice before attacking.
levels.why: It matters because when more countries join in, a fight can grow.

levels.headline: A promise between three friends
levels.body:
Imagine three friends who make a promise. If anyone bothers one of them, the other two will help. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are three countries that have made a promise like that. It is called the Mecca defence pact.
This week, a group called the Houthis, from a country next door called Yemen, attacked places in Saudi Arabia. The Houthis say they hit an airport and an oil refinery. So the three friends met, and they agreed to send soldiers and equipment to Saudi Arabia quickly.
It is like a big group of friends turning up in the playground. They hope it will stop anyone from picking on their friend again.
It is very serious, because real soldiers are involved.
levels.why: It matters because it shows how countries look after each other, and how fights can spread.

headline: Zelenskiy warns of massive Russian attack as Ukraine vows to hit more refineries

terms.meaning: A factory that turns crude oil into fuels such as petrol and diesel.
Secret information gathered about what an enemy is planning.
Systems that shoot down incoming missiles, drones and aircraft.

levels.headline: Zelenskiy warns of massive Russian attack as Ukraine vows to hit more refineries
levels.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy has said updated intelligence shows Russia is preparing a massive attack on Ukraine, and that Ukraine will step up its strikes on Russian oil refineries in response.
He said Ukraine's services and air force are ready to respond within the limits of the air defence resources available. Ukrainian intelligence has obtained documents showing that President Putin has told his military to broaden attacks on civilian targets before the winter, which Mr Zelenskiy described as a new Russian doctrine aimed at forcing people to flee Kyiv and other cities.
Russia's Defence Ministry said strikes on military and military-industrial targets and related infrastructure in Kyiv and other regions will be intensified.
The exchange suggests that energy infrastructure on both sides will be a central target as winter approaches.
levels.why: Attacks on energy and cities affect civilians, and strikes on refineries can influence fuel supplies and prices.

levels.headline: Zelenskiy says Russia is preparing a major attack; Kyiv to hit refineries harder
levels.body:
President Volodymyr Zelenskiy has said updated intelligence indicates Russia is preparing a massive attack, and that Ukraine will intensify strikes on Russian oil refineries.
He said Ukraine's intelligence services and air force are ready to respond within the limits of their air defence resources. Ukrainian services say they have documents showing President Putin has ordered the military to widen attacks on civilian targets before winter, which Mr Zelenskiy called a new doctrine intended to push people out of Kyiv and other cities.
Russia's Defence Ministry has said its strikes on military and military-industrial sites and related infrastructure in Kyiv and other regions will be stepped up.
Both sides therefore appear set to target energy and infrastructure as the cold weather arrives.
levels.why: Winter attacks on infrastructure put civilians at risk and can affect global fuel markets.

levels.headline: Ukraine expects a big Russian attack and promises to hit oil refineries
levels.body:
Ukraine's President, Volodymyr Zelenskiy, says new intelligence shows Russia is getting ready for a massive attack. He also says Ukraine will hit more Russian oil refineries.
He said Ukraine's services and air force are ready to respond, but they are limited by how much air defence equipment they have. Ukrainian intelligence says it has documents showing Russia's president, Vladimir Putin, has told the military to attack more civilian targets before winter. Mr Zelenskiy says this is a new plan to make people leave Kyiv and other cities.
Russia's Defence Ministry says it will increase strikes on military and related targets in Kyiv and other regions.
Winter is coming, so attacks on energy are expected to be a big part of the fighting.
levels.why: It matters because ordinary people in cities could lose power and heating, and fuel supplies could be affected.

levels.headline: Zelenskiy says Russia plans a big attack as Ukraine targets refineries
levels.body:
Ukraine's President, Volodymyr Zelenskiy, says the latest intelligence shows Russia is planning a massive attack. He says Ukraine will respond by hitting more Russian oil refineries.
He said Ukraine's intelligence services and air force are ready to respond as far as their air defence equipment allows. Ukrainian officials say they have papers showing that Vladimir Putin has told his military to attack more civilian targets before winter. Mr Zelenskiy called this a new Russian doctrine aimed at driving people out of Kyiv and other cities.
Russia's Defence Ministry says it will step up strikes in Kyiv and other regions on military and related targets.
With winter near, attacks on energy sites are likely to continue on both sides.
levels.why: It matters because winter attacks on energy can leave people cold, and refinery strikes can affect fuel supplies.

levels.headline: Ukraine says Russia is planning a big attack
levels.body:
Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskiy, says secret information shows that Russia is planning a very big attack. This kind of secret information is called intelligence.
He says Ukraine's army and air force are ready, but they only have a limited amount of equipment to shoot down missiles and drones. Ukrainian officials also say they have papers showing that Russia's president, Vladimir Putin, wants his army to attack more places where ordinary people live before winter. Mr Zelenskiy says Russia wants to make people leave Kyiv and other cities.
Ukraine says it will hit more Russian oil refineries in return. A refinery is a factory that turns oil into fuel. Russia says it will attack more places in Kyiv and other regions.
levels.why: It matters because winter is coming, and attacks on power and fuel can hurt ordinary people.

levels.headline: Ukraine warns Russia is planning a huge attack
levels.body:
Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskiy, says secret information, called intelligence, shows that Russia is planning a massive attack. He says Ukraine's army and air force are ready, but they can only use the air defence equipment that they have.
Ukrainian officials also say they have documents showing that Russia's president, Vladimir Putin, wants his military to attack more places where civilians live before winter. Mr Zelenskiy says this is a new Russian plan to make people flee Kyiv and other cities.
Ukraine says it will answer by hitting more Russian oil refineries, which are factories that turn oil into fuel. Russia's Defence Ministry says it will increase its strikes on military and related targets in Kyiv and other regions.
With winter near, attacks on energy sites are expected to continue.
levels.why: It matters because people need heating and light in winter, and fuel supplies can be affected.

levels.headline: Ukraine and Russia warn of more attacks
levels.body:
Ukraine and Russia have been at war for a long time. Now both sides say they will attack more.
Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskiy, says his country has secret information about what Russia is planning. This secret information is called intelligence. He says Russia is getting ready for a very big attack. He also says Russia wants to make people leave Kyiv and other cities before winter by attacking places where people live.
He says Ukraine will answer by attacking more Russian oil refineries. A refinery is a factory that makes fuel from oil.
Russia says it will attack more places in Kyiv and other regions.
As it gets colder, both sides are likely to aim at power and fuel.
levels.why: It matters because people need heat and light in winter, and fuel supplies could be affected.

levels.headline: A war gets more serious before winter
levels.body:
Ukraine and Russia are two countries that are fighting a war. Now, with winter coming, both say they will attack more.
The president of Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelenskiy, says he has secret news. It says Russia is getting ready for a very big attack. He says Russia wants to scare people into leaving cities like Kyiv.
Ukraine says it will hit back by attacking Russian oil refineries. A refinery is a big factory where oil is turned into fuel for cars and for heating.
Russia says it will attack more places in Kyiv and other areas, too.
People who live in cities are worried. In winter, it is very hard to be without heat and light.
levels.why: It matters because ordinary families are caught in the war, and winter makes things harder.

levels.headline: A very serious fight
levels.body:
Ukraine and Russia are countries that are fighting each other in a war. It is very sad and scary for the people who live there.
The leader of Ukraine says he has heard that Russia is planning a big attack. Winter is coming, and it gets very cold there. He says Russia wants to make people leave their homes in the cities.
Ukraine says it will hit back by attacking places in Russia that make fuel from oil. These places are called refineries. Russia says it will attack more places in Ukraine too.
When it is cold, families need heat and light. That is why people are worried about what happens next.
levels.why: It matters because families need to stay warm and safe.

levels.headline: Staying safe when it gets cold
levels.body:
Imagine it is a freezing winter and your school is having a big argument between two groups. Now imagine the argument gets louder and louder.
That is a bit like what is happening between Ukraine and Russia. They are countries and they are fighting a war. The leader of Ukraine says Russia is getting ready for a big attack as winter comes. He says Russia wants to scare people out of their homes in the cities.
Ukraine says it will answer by attacking Russian factories that turn oil into fuel. Russia says it will attack more places, too.
In the cold, everybody needs heat and light to stay safe. That is why this is so serious.
levels.why: It matters because everyone needs to be warm and safe in winter.

headline: Fed raises interest rates to 3.75%-4%, first increase since 2023

terms.meaning: The central bank of the United States, which sets the country's main interest rate.
A decision to raise interest rates, making borrowing more expensive.
One hundredth of a percentage point.

levels.headline: Fed raises interest rates to 3.75%-4%, first increase since 2023
levels.body:
The US Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to a target range of 3.75% to 4% on 16 September, its first increase since 2023.
The Federal Open Market Committee approved the move unanimously. The Fed said it was acting to fight inflation pushed up by surging oil prices and other factors. Chairman Kevin Warsh told a news conference that inflation has been too high for too long.
The committee's statement said economic activity is expanding at a solid pace, spending has been resilient, productivity growth is strong and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and unemployment has changed little.
Updated projections point to the possibility of another increase this year, and markets expect one more 25 basis point rise in 2026, followed by further rises into 2027.
levels.why: US interest rates influence borrowing costs and markets across the world, including in the UK.

levels.headline: Federal Reserve lifts rates to 3.75%-4% in first hike since 2023
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve raised its main interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point on 16 September, to a range of 3.75% to 4%. It is the first rise since 2023.
The decision was unanimous. The Fed said the move was aimed at tackling inflation caused by sharply higher oil prices and other pressures. Its chairman, Kevin Warsh, said inflation has been too high for too long.
The Fed described the economy as expanding at a solid pace, with resilient spending, strong productivity growth and robust investment. Job gains have kept up with the workforce.
Officials signalled that one more rise is possible this year, and financial markets expect a further quarter-point increase in 2026 and more in 2027.
levels.why: The world's biggest central bank is tightening policy while the Bank of England is on hold.

levels.headline: US central bank raises interest rates for the first time since 2023
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve, the US central bank, raised its main interest rate on 16 September. It went up by a quarter of a percentage point, to a range of 3.75% to 4%. It is the first increase since 2023.
All the members of the committee voted for the rise. The Fed says it wants to fight inflation, which has been driven up by surging oil prices. Chairman Kevin Warsh said inflation has been too high for too long.
The Fed said the economy is growing at a solid pace, people are still spending, and there are enough jobs for the people looking. Updated forecasts suggest there could be one more rate rise this year.
Investors expect rates to keep rising into 2027.
levels.why: It matters because US rates affect borrowing costs and investment around the world.

levels.headline: The Fed puts up interest rates for the first time in three years
levels.body:
The US Federal Reserve has raised interest rates by 0.25 percentage points. They are now between 3.75% and 4%. This is the first rise since 2023.
Everyone on the committee voted for it. The Fed is trying to bring down inflation, which has risen because of high oil prices. The Fed's chairman, Kevin Warsh, said inflation has been too high for too long.
The Fed said that the US economy is growing steadily. People are still spending, businesses are investing and there are enough jobs. It thinks there may be one more rate rise before the end of the year.
Investors expect more rises to come next year.
levels.why: It matters because what the US does with rates affects mortgages, loans and markets in many countries.

levels.headline: America's central bank puts up interest rates
levels.body:
America's central bank, the Federal Reserve, raised its main interest rate on 16 September by a quarter of a percentage point. It now stands between 3.75% and 4%. It is the first rise since 2023, and every member of the committee voted for it.
The Fed said it wants to fight inflation, which means prices rising too fast. It said oil prices have surged and that has pushed up inflation. The Fed's chairman, Kevin Warsh, said inflation has been too high for too long.
The Fed said that the US economy is expanding at a solid pace and that people are still spending. It also said there are enough jobs for people who want them.
Officials think one more rise is possible this year, and investors expect rises to continue into 2027.
levels.why: It matters because US interest rates influence the cost of borrowing in many countries.

levels.headline: America's central bank has raised interest rates
levels.body:
America has a central bank called the Federal Reserve, or the Fed. It sets an interest rate. This rate makes borrowing money cost more or less. On 16 September, the Fed raised the rate a little. It is now between 3.75% and 4%. It is the first rise since 2023.
The Fed did this because prices are rising too fast. Oil has become very expensive, and that has pushed up prices. The head of the Fed, Kevin Warsh, said prices have been rising too fast for too long. Everyone on the committee agreed.
The Fed says the US economy is still doing well, with people spending and enough jobs.
It may raise the rate one more time this year.
levels.why: It matters because raising rates can slow prices, but it makes loans cost more.

levels.headline: US interest rates go up for the first time in three years
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States. Its job is to keep prices steady. It does this by changing an interest rate. A higher rate makes loans cost more and saving pay more.
On 16 September, the Fed raised the rate by a small amount, to between 3.75% and 4%. It is the first time it has gone up since 2023. Everyone on the committee voted yes.
The reason is that prices have been going up too fast. Oil is very expensive, which pushes up the cost of lots of things. The head of the Fed, Kevin Warsh, said this has happened for too long.
The Fed thinks the US economy is strong. It may raise the rate once more this year.
levels.why: It matters because what happens in the US can change borrowing costs in other countries too.

levels.headline: America raises its interest rate
levels.body:
A bank for banks can change how expensive it is to borrow money. In America, that bank is called the Federal Reserve. It has just made borrowing a little more expensive. The rate it sets went up to somewhere between 3.75% and 4%. It had not gone up for a few years.
The Fed did this because prices have been going up too fast. Oil costs a lot at the moment, and that makes lots of things cost more. The head of the Fed, Kevin Warsh, said prices have been too high for too long.
The people who make the decision all agreed. They think the American economy is strong.
They say they may raise the rate one more time this year.
levels.why: It matters because it changes how costly loans are, and that affects many people.

levels.headline: Why a bank changed its rate
levels.body:
Imagine a big bank that looks after a whole country's money. It has a special dial called the interest rate. If it turns the dial up, borrowing costs more, and people tend to spend less. That can slow down price rises.
In America, this bank is called the Federal Reserve. On 16 September, it turned the dial up a little. The rate is now between 3.75% and 4%. It had not turned it up since 2023.
The Fed did it because prices have been going up too fast. Oil is very expensive, and that makes many things cost more. The boss of the Fed, Kevin Warsh, said prices have been high for too long.
Everyone on the team agreed.
levels.why: It matters because it can slow price rises, but it makes borrowing cost more.

levels.headline: A tool to slow down prices
levels.body:
Imagine a shop where sweets keep getting more and more expensive. Somebody has to try to slow it down. In America, that job belongs to a group called the Federal Reserve.
The Fed has a tool called an interest rate. When the rate goes up, borrowing money costs more, so people tend to spend a little less. This helps slow down price rises.
On 16 September, the Fed raised the rate a little, to between 3.75% and 4%. It had not done this for years. They did it because prices have been going up too quickly, partly because oil costs so much now.
The boss of the Fed, Kevin Warsh, said the problem had gone on too long.
levels.why: It matters because it helps keep prices steady, but it makes borrowing cost more.

headline: S&P 500 hits record high as oil prices ease and tech leads

terms.meaning: An index tracking the share prices of 500 of the biggest companies listed in the US.
The main international benchmark price for oil.
The return investors get from lending to the US government; it moves with interest rate expectations.

levels.headline: S&P 500 hits record high as oil prices ease and tech leads
levels.body:
The S&P 500 set a new record on Tuesday 6 October, closing at 7,818.93, up 44.98 points or 0.58%. The Nasdaq Composite also rose, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed at 51,521.28, up 253.38 points or 0.49%.
Technology shares led the rally for another day. Easing oil prices and lower Treasury yields helped, and investors turned their attention to company earnings growth. Optimism over a nuclear power deal between Constellation Energy and Alphabet, Google's parent company, also lifted nuclear stocks.
Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, was trading at about $101 a barrel. US crude fell by about 1.6% to around $88.
Strong share prices contrast with higher prices for consumers and rising interest rates in the US.
levels.why: Record share prices affect pensions and savings, while high oil prices continue to pressure household budgets.

levels.headline: Wall Street record as tech surges and oil eases
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed at a record 7,818.93 on 6 October, a rise of 0.58%. The Nasdaq Composite also gained, and the Dow Jones ended at 51,521.28, up 0.49%.
Technology companies led the way again. Lower oil prices and falling Treasury yields helped sentiment, so investors looked more at earnings growth. Hopes of a nuclear power deal between Constellation Energy and Alphabet pushed nuclear stocks higher.
Brent crude traded near $101 a barrel, while US crude slipped roughly 1.6% to about $88.
The rally comes while higher energy prices are lifting inflation and the Federal Reserve has begun raising interest rates.
levels.why: Markets are rising even as inflation and energy costs remain worries for consumers.

levels.headline: US shares reach another record while oil prices ease
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed at a new record high of 7,818.93 on 6 October, up 0.58%. The Nasdaq also rose, and the Dow Jones finished at 51,521.28, up 0.49%.
Technology firms led the gains again. Oil prices fell back a little and the return on US government borrowing, called Treasury yields, eased. That left investors free to focus on company profits. Excitement about a nuclear power deal between Constellation Energy and Alphabet, the owner of Google, boosted nuclear companies.
Brent crude, the international oil price, was about $101 a barrel. US crude fell about 1.6% to nearly $88.
Share prices are high even though energy costs are pushing up prices for ordinary people.
levels.why: It matters because share prices affect savings and pensions, while oil prices affect everyday costs.

levels.headline: Record day for US shares as tech leads and oil eases
levels.body:
The S&P 500 index of big US companies ended Tuesday at a record 7,818.93, up 0.58%. The Nasdaq also rose, and the Dow Jones ended at 51,521.28, up 0.49%.
Tech companies led the climb once more. Oil prices eased and US government borrowing costs, known as Treasury yields, fell. Investors then paid more attention to company profits. News of a possible nuclear power deal between Constellation Energy and Alphabet, which owns Google, lifted nuclear companies.
Brent crude, which is used as the world oil price, was around $101 a barrel. US crude dropped about 1.6% to nearly $88.
Shares are rising even though energy costs are making life dearer for families.
levels.why: It matters because stock markets affect savings and pensions, and oil prices affect what people pay.

levels.headline: US shares hit a record as oil prices ease
levels.body:
Share prices in the United States reached a new high on Tuesday 6 October. The S&P 500, which follows 500 of the biggest US companies, closed at 7,818.93, up 0.58% on the day. The Dow Jones, another measure of the market, closed at 51,521.28, up 0.49%.
Technology companies did best. Oil prices eased a little, and the return on US government borrowing, called Treasury yields, also fell. This helped investors to focus on company profits. News of a possible nuclear power deal between Constellation Energy and Alphabet, which owns Google, helped nuclear companies too.
Oil is still dear. Brent crude, the world price, was about $101 a barrel.
So shares are rising, but energy costs are still high for families.
levels.why: It matters because share prices affect savings and pensions, and oil costs affect everyday bills.

levels.headline: US share prices hit a new high
levels.body:
Share prices show how much people think companies are worth. On Tuesday 6 October, a well-known measure of 500 big American companies, called the S&P 500, hit a record high. It ended the day at 7,818.93, which was 0.58% more than the day before. The Dow Jones, another measure, also rose by 0.49%.
Companies that make technology led the way. Oil prices fell back a little, which made investors happier. There was also good news for nuclear power firms. Constellation Energy and Alphabet, the company that owns Google, are reported to be working on a nuclear power deal.
Oil is still dear. The world price is about $101 a barrel.
levels.why: It matters because share prices affect people's savings and pensions.

levels.headline: Share prices in the US reach a record
levels.body:
When people buy shares, they buy a small piece of a company. The prices of shares change every day. On Tuesday 6 October, a list of 500 big American companies, called the S&P 500, hit its highest ever level. It rose by 0.58% in one day.
Companies that make technology did best. Oil became a little cheaper, and that helped. News about a nuclear power deal between two big companies, Constellation Energy and Alphabet, which owns Google, also made investors happy.
But oil is still very expensive. The world price is about $101 a barrel. That is a lot more than before the Iran war began to cause problems.
So shares are high, and oil costs are high too.
levels.why: It matters because share prices affect savings, and oil costs affect families.

levels.headline: A record day for shares
levels.body:
Companies sell small pieces of themselves. These are called shares. People buy them hoping they will become more valuable. On Tuesday 6 October, shares in America did very well. A group of 500 big companies, called the S&P 500, reached its highest level ever.
Technology companies did best. Oil became a little cheaper, and that helped. People were also excited about a possible deal on nuclear power between two big companies, Constellation Energy and Alphabet, which owns Google.
Oil is still very expensive, though. It costs about $101 a barrel. That is a lot more than people would like.
So while some people are happy about shares, other people worry about how much things cost.
levels.why: It matters because shares affect savings, while oil costs affect what everyone pays.

levels.headline: Shares go up and up
levels.body:
A share is a tiny piece of a company. If the company does well, the share can be worth more. On Tuesday 6 October, shares in American companies reached the highest level ever. A list of 500 big companies, called the S&P 500, had its best day yet.
Companies that make computers and phones did well. A deal about nuclear power between two companies made people excited, too.
Oil, which makes petrol, is still very pricey. It costs about $101 a barrel. A barrel is a big container for oil.
So some people feel happy because their shares are worth more. Other people worry because things cost more.
levels.why: It matters because shares can change how much money people have saved.

levels.headline: Collecting stickers
levels.body:
Imagine everyone in your class collects football stickers. If a sticker becomes very popular, other children will pay more for it. Its price goes up.
Shares work a bit like that. A share is a tiny piece of a company. If lots of people want it, the price goes up. On Tuesday 6 October, prices for lots of big American companies went up to the highest level ever. That is because people think the companies will do well.
But oil, which is used to make petrol, is also costing a lot. It is about $101 for one big barrel.
So the stickers are worth more, but petrol is still pricey.
levels.why: It matters because people's savings can go up with shares, but their bills can go up with oil.
